records.name: Minjona
records.facts_used: Minjona: Siliņš connects the name with French mignon, gentle, cute or darling. Internationally Mignon is also known as a literary character’s name. The adjective and the character’s history are connected, but do not determine why every family chose Latvian Minjona. Siliņš’s dictionary dates the use of Minjona: possibly the last quarter of the nineteenth century. Its calendar year is 1915. This records use of the particular name in Latvia. The entry cannot automatically be transferred to similar spellings or treated as the moment the entire name family originated.

records.uncertainties: Siliņš p 241 Frenchmignon and ownpossiblelastquarter 19 c/calendar 1915; uncertainty of earliestattestation retained. No claim every Latvianbearer namedafter Goethe.

records.name: Artemida
records.facts_used: Artemida: The exact form is connected with Greek Artemis, also known as the hunting goddess’s name. The further meaning of Artemis is not securely established. Popular comparisons with safe or bear are therefore not presented as a proved translation. The Latvian Language Agency gives the exact rendering Άρτεμις → Artemida, citing page 33 of a 2015 manual. This dated record illustrates transmission between languages; it is not a first birth registration or proof of one borrowing route in every family.

records.name: Dominykas
records.facts_used: Dominykas: Lithuanian Dominykas continues Latin Dominicus, of the Lord, from dominus, lord. The family is also linked to Sunday’s name and a tradition of naming children born that day, without determining every bearer’s day of birth. The medieval name dictionary gives related Latin Dominicus in France in 814. This is earlier evidence for the international family, rather than the first Lithuanian registration of Dominykas or its year of invention.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.

records.name: Teofilis
records.facts_used: Teofilis: The name belongs to the Greek Theophilos family, with theos, god, and philos, beloved or dear. These explain the two ancient name elements. The Lithuanian form retains that connection without determining a modern bearer’s religion. The medieval name dictionary records related Theophilus in England in 1578. This is a dated foreign example of the family. It cannot be turned into a first-use date for the exact Lithuanian spelling Teofilis.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: DMNESEngland Early Modern English 1578 Theophilus Reg Patp 33; exactguide Greekstemroute. Salys July 22 recordnotusedas December 20 membershipauthority.

records.name: Pärja
records.facts_used: Pärja: The Estonian given name was formed from pärg, wreath. The dictionary gives this derivation specifically for the personal name, and the local name column repeats it. It is distinct from an explanation based only on an accidentally similar foreign word. Page 18 of Mägiste’s 1929 name list gives Pärja in the female-name list. This is specific dated evidence for the local form. The dictionary’s publication year is not the name’s invention date or a first birth record.
